episodes.215070: Very warm temperatures on the afternoon of the eighth along with a mid-level moisture plume overhead created isolated thunderstorms over the Rolling Plains. A very dry sub-cloud layer allowed these storms to have high cloud bases and produce strong wind gusts. One of these storms produced a severe wind gust near McAdoo (Dickens County).
episodes.215075: Monsoonal moisture funneled northward into the Desert Southwest as the main monsoon high slid eastward over TX. This allowed for a greater coverage of locally heavy rain producing afternoon showers and thunderstorms across western and parts of central NM August 12th. One such storm produced flash flooding in the Coyote Canyon-Nizhoni Housing neighborhood along W. Navajo Service Route 9 in Brimhall during the evening hours.
episodes.215082: Around 3:00 pm CDT on August 13, a microburst occurred in the eastern part of the city of Opelika, resulting in numerous downed trees and power lines, along with reports of small hail.
episodes.215100: Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 13th and a weakening upper level ridge allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop across the central South Plains. A very dry sub-cloud layer caused these storms to produce wet microbursts across the region. A few Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites observed a couple of these microbursts recording severe level winds.
episodes.215105: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the Ohio Valley during a 36 hour period. Widespread wind damage occurred due to strong storms. Between 8 to 11 inches of rain fell across eastern Indiana, resulting in historic flooding in spots.
episodes.215140: From the 13th afternoon through the 14th midday, multiple rounds of severe weather and training thunderstorms impacted central Indiana. A moist and unstable airmass, characterized by abundant low-level moisture and strong instability along remnant boundaries, supported the initial development of organized multicell clusters. Anomalous moisture and slow storm motions over antecedent saturated ground subsequently favored cell training, creating conditions conducive for localized flash flooding. Strong instability and enhanced deep-layer wind shear also supported severe thunderstorms which produced damaging winds and large hail.||Convection initially developed during the mid-to-late afternoon of August 13 across west-central Indiana, tracking eastward across Vermillion, Parke, Vigo, Clay, and Bartholomew counties between 15:26 and 17:05 EST. Severe thunderstorm wind gusts reached 58 to 65 mph, with estimated localized gusts of 60 to 70 mph in Vigo County. These winds uprooted numerous trees, severed power lines, ignited a power line fire, snapped at least ten utility poles in Bartholomew County, and caused roof and structural damage to residences in Vermillion County. A secondary round of severe activity intensified late that evening across east-central Indiana, where storms produced quarter to golf ball-sized hail (1.00 to 1.75 inches in diameter) and wind gusts up to 64 mph across Madison and Delaware counties, downing trees onto residences and vehicles and causing damage to corn crops.||During the overnight and early morning hours of August 14, repeated rounds of training storms generated localized rainfall totals ranging from 2.0 to 5.3 inches over saturated soils, triggering significant flash flooding across Madison, Randolph, Tipton, Vermillion, and Warren counties. Floodwaters forced multiple roadway closures, including sections of State Road 28 and U.S. Highway 31, submerged more than ten roads with flowing water in Farmland, and caused a streambank washout along Eagle Branch Creek behind a manufactured home park. In Warren County, an overflowing ditch inundated roadways and washed a vehicle into a drainage ditch, necessitating an emergency water rescue.
episodes.215142: On the 11-15th, several rounds of heavy to extreme rainfall within the upper White River watershed led to major flooding from Muncie to Indianapolis on both the White River and several tributaries.  One-day rainfall amounts:  through the early morning of the 12th were as great as 4-8 inches across all watershed areas east of Anderson; through the early morning of the 13th were up to 2-5 inches for most areas near and east of Anderson; with subsequent, less intense rains focused from the Tipton to Anderson areas;  leading to widespread 5-day totals through the 15th evening of 5-10 inches from northern Marion County to all watershed points north and east, including a large area of 9-13 inches from Anderson to the White River's easternmost headwaters in Randolph County.||Resultant major flooding impacted all points on the upper White River from Muncie down to Ravenswood, with the crest advancing from Muncie on the 13th midday to Ravenswood by the 15th late day;  including record crests at both Anderson (24.93 feet, surpassing 23.60 from 3/23/1904) and Noblesville (24.60 feet, surpassing 23.80 from 3/25/1913).  Significant flooding was ubiquitous over several White River tributaries, including crests in major flood on Fall Creek at Fortville (13th evening) and Cicero Creek at Arcadia (15th late day).||Flooding impacts ranged from evacuations in the Muncie and Indianapolis areas, to submerged roadways and highways in Delaware County and the Anderson and Edgewood parts of Madison County;  and inundated residential neighborhoods in Muncie, Yorktown, Riverwood, Noblesville, Federal Hill, low-lying portions of Fishers and Carmel, Ravenswood, Rocky Ripple and near Broad Ripple.  Ninety swift water rescues were needed in Hamilton County, and emergency floodgate operations were needed in northern Marion County. Approximately 2,500 structures were impacted across Delaware, Hamilton, Madison and Marion Counties.  Most notably the White River in Carmel flooded back up Blue Woods Creek, washing out the Hazel Dell Parkway bridge and overflowing as a waterfall into the Martin Marietta - North Indianapolis Mine.  Two fatalities occurred in Delaware County.||Outside of the broader river flooding, a culvert washout caused a fatality in Henry County after the flash flooding ended when a bicycler rode into the collapsed road and perished.
episodes.215246: A slow-moving storm system brought moderate to heavy rain to multiple locations over the course of two days. A recent dry spell and local drought impacts were able to absorb most of the rainfall. Aside from rainfall measurements, no additional impacts were reported.
episodes.215346: Scattered thunderstorms moved through southern New England in the evening but only caused a few wind damage reports in southeast MA.
episodes.215549: A cool cyclonic flow of unstable air moved across northern NY and VT during the afternoon and evening hours of August 12th. Scattered showers and thunderstorms occurred across the area with just a few storms in south-central VT producing isolated severe weather.
episodes.215762: Widely scattered thunderstorms developed across portions of central Kansas during the late afternoon and evening hours of August 13th. The individual thunderstorms were quite brief but produced severe caliber winds as they weakened. Damage was produced to power poles in Reno County near Partridge with up to a half mile stretch down. A microburst led to a rolled semi trailer in Russell County along Interstate 70; the driver was transported with minor injuries. There were two measured wind gusts of 77 mph at Great Bend Airport and Hutchinson Municipal Airport.
episodes.216053: Primarily scattered thunderstorm wind damage occurred with northwest flow convection along and south of the I-26 corridor. A favorable environment was in place with MLCAPE values from 2000-3000 J/kg and DCAPE values around 1000 J/kg. Weak shortwave energy moving through the northwest flow helped initiate convection within the unstable environment.
episodes.216087: Severe thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado. Strong winds up to 81 mph were reported with the thunderstorms with several gusts of 55 to 75 mph being reported.
episodes.216092: Isolated severe thunderstorms developed over northeast Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours. A storm brought golf ball sized hail and heavy rain to the southeast part of the Denver metro area. Elsewhere, strong winds were the main form of severe weather with a peak wind of 71 mph in Weld County. Flooding was also reported in Greeley near the intersection of highways 85 and 34.
episodes.216133: A surface trough and nearby shortwave caused thunderstorms to develop across mainly northern and western portions of the Permian Basin. Meanwhile, upslope flow also aided in the development of storms in the Davis Mountains and Stockton Plateau. A couple of these storms were able to produce severe wind gusts.
episodes.216139: A bowing line of thunderstorms tracked along the I-74 corridor, producing widespread wind damage from Tazewell County southeastward to Edgar County during the afternoon of August 13th.  Some of the most significant damage occurred in Bloomington-Normal where part of the roof was torn off the OSF St. Joseph Hospital.  Isolated flash flooding occurred as well.
episodes.216142: During the afternoon and early evening hours on the 12th, several clusters of strong to locally severe thunderstorms materialized across portions of southwest and south-central AZ. Thunderstorms began to develop first across southwestern AZ, with the more concentrated activity centered in La Paz County, especially near the town of Quartzsite, where training thunderstorms cells materialized. These training thunderstorms caused significant rainfall accumulations of 2-4 inches as estimated by doppler radar and resulted in extensive flooding across much of Quartzsite. Additional thunderstorm cells developed across portions of south-central AZ, including the Phoenix Metro Area, where locally damaging winds were observed. Atmospheric conditions prior to storm initiation were highly conducive for strong convective development across the region. Pre-storm mesoscale analysis revealed abundant moisture in place throughout the area, with precipitable water values surpassing 1.5 inches. Coupled with colder than normal 500 mb temperatures around -6 to -7��C, this deep moisture fueled moderate-to-strong atmospheric instability, with MLCAPE values ranging between 1000 and 2000 J/kg. Alongside the favorable thermodynamic support, broad dynamic forcing was present thanks to a large-scale low pressure system positioned off the West Coast, which provided upper-level speed divergence to sustain and increase thunderstorm coverage across the area.
episodes.216143: During the mid-afternoon hours on the 12th, a cluster of severe thunderstorms materialized near the International Border, just south of El Centro with peak wind gusts likely exceeding 60 mph. Major damage to the electrical infrastructure was observed as over 150 power poles were compromised, resulting in over 5000 customers losing power at one point. There was also some other wind damage reports, including some downed trees and a large billboard toppled. Heavy rainfall from the thunderstorm cluster also resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding, with 1-2 falling within an hour according to doppler radar estimates. Strong outflow winds generated a large dust storm that surged northward through western Imperial County and into portions of Riverside County, including moving across the Salton Sea and Coachella Valley to the northwest. The overall environment that this thunderstorm cluster developed under was characterized by strong instability with MLCAPE values peaking at 2000 J/KG along with high Precipitable Water Values in excess of 1.7, supporting the potential for heavy rainfall. Alongside the favorable thermodynamic support, broad dynamic forcing was present thanks to a large-scale low pressure system positioned off the West Coast, which provided upper-level speed divergence to enhance the thunderstorm activity.
episodes.216238: A train of systems brought rounds of heavy downpours and strong to severe thunderstorms across the area while a frontal boundary wavered over northern Ohio and the Great Lakes region. A combination of very heavy rain and training storms led to flooding across portions of southeast Ohio and West Virginia.||Storms first originated in the Midwest during this time period, producing a long stretch of storm damage that encompassed the Ohio Valley into the Central Appalachians. Little to no time for atmospheric recovery was allotted before the next round of strong storms plagued the area. As a result, these episodic rounds of storms produced thousands of dollars in damage caused by powerful winds and heavy downpours. 72-hour rainfall amounts ranged from one to three inches in Gallia, Jackson, Lawrence, Meigs, and Vinton Counties and five to eight inches in Athens, Washington, Morgan, and Perry Counties. The heaviest amounts were observed in Perry and Morgan Counties, which set forth devastating flooding to the region. In addition to numerous flooded roads, water rescues, and rises on local creeks and streams, river gauges recorded flooding on Sunday Creek at Glouster, the Muskingum River at Beverly, and the Hocking River at Athens.
episodes.216243: Following a very active start to the month, waves of heavy rain and severe thunderstorms continued to impact the area as a frontal boundary lifted into and then remained present over the Middle Ohio Valley through mid-August. ||A combination of very heavy rain and back-building or training storms resulted in additional flooding across portions of southeast Ohio, southwest Virginia, and West Virginia. 48-hour rainfall amounts ranged from one to four inches in parts of southwest Virginia, which resulted in flooded roads and minor flooding on the Pound River at Norland. In regards to the severe aspect of storms during this timeframe, only two instances of storm damage was noted in southwest Virginia, while the bulk of the damage took place north of the state line.
episodes.216404: On the 12th, sub-tropical moisture continued to increase over western NV, leading to widespread shower and thunderstorm coverage. The Sierra Front experienced areas of flash flooding during the afternoon, with Reno International Airport setting a new daily rainfall record of 0.60 inches.
episodes.216405: On the 13th, with abundant moisture over the region, the area experienced the most widespread thunderstorm coverage. A total of 8 Severe Thunderstorm Warnings and one Tornado Warning (not confirmed) were issued during the afternoon. There were multiple reports of flash flooding across western NV, along with wind damage in Schurz.
episodes.216694: During the evenings on 08/13 and 08/14, isolated severe storms formed along a stationary boundary.  Reports of damaging wind gusts up to 80 mph and wind damage were reported. Storms on the 14th and 15th produced multiple downburst winds from northern Shawnee into Jefferson counties were multiple homes and trees were damaged. Wind gusts were estimated in excess of 90 mph.
episodes.216799: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.
episodes.216819: Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the mid to late afternoon hours between Gila Bend and Casa Grande in south-central AZ. The overall synoptic pattern was characterized by a broad upper-level trough situated along the west coast, providing some upper-level forcing for ascent. The thermodynamic environment was characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/KG with DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/KG as well, supporting the potential for strong downburst wind gusts. Wind damage in the form of  downed power poles near the vicinity of I-8 just west of Gila Bend and in Arizona City were observed. Outflows from these storms also produced areas of locally dense blowing dust with visibilities briefly dropping to under a quarter mile.
episodes.216826: A strong thunderstorm briefly produced high winds in south central South Dakota. A resident in Westover reported that a dead tree had been downed, along with several large branches.
episodes.216837: Flooding was observed after heavy rainfall in and around the town of Highmore, with standing water reported in fields and a number of county roads underwater and closed. The Hyde county Emergency Manager tallied 7.3 inches of moisture 2 south of Highmore, while the COOP observer in Highmore measured 5.65 inches of moisture. The South Dakota State University mesonet station just outside of Highmore likewise recorded 5.03 inches of moisture.
episodes.217007: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.  Heavy rain resulted in localized flash flooding in Irwin county.
episodes.217210: Very heavy rainfall impacted parts of the region during the early morning hours of August 12. Several counties in eastern Indiana had the greatest impacts, with rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches. Some locations in northern and western Wayne County, received close to 10 inches of rain. This rainfall led to significant rises on the Whitewater River, which continued into August 14.
episodes.217242: A disturbance moved into the region from the Great Lakes during the late afternoon and evening, bringing scattered thunderstorms into the overnight hours. Despite limited surface instability, significant elevated instability supported development of scattered damaging hail and isolated strong wind gusts.
episodes.217243: A disturbance moved into the region from the Great Lakes during the late afternoon and evening, bringing scattered thunderstorms into the overnight hours. Despite limited surface instability, significant elevated instability supported stronger thunderstorms capable of producing hail and isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.217374: On the 13th, with abundant sub-tropical moisture over the region, we experienced the most widespread thunderstorm coverage over the eastern Sierra, especially in Mono County.
episodes.217384: During the early morning hours of August 13, 2026, a severe nocturnal thunderstorm complex swept east-northeast across portions of east-central and northeast Nebraska, impacting Boone, Platte, Madison, Stanton, Colfax, and Cuming counties. Propelled by strong low-level shear and robust atmospheric instability. The complex produced a quick round of heavy rainfall in Monona county, bringing flash flooding. Peak rainfall rates of 2.00 to 2.50 inches per hour quickly produced total accumulations of 2.00 to 3.50 inches across northern and central Monona County. County officials reported street damage with asphalt torn up due to heavy rain and flash flooding in Mapleton, IA. Flooding was also noted at the sewer plant.
episodes.217385: During the early morning hours of August 13, 2026, a severe nocturnal thunderstorm complex swept east-northeast across portions of east-central and northeast Nebraska, impacting Boone, Platte, Madison, Stanton, Colfax, and Cuming counties. Propelled by strong low-level shear and robust atmospheric instability, the complex produced a widespread swath of destructive straight-line winds accompanied by several embedded tornadoes. The overall storm corridor produced severe wind gusts between 60 and 90 mph and causing extensive damage to trees, utility lines, agricultural structures, and crops.||National Weather Service storm surveys confirmed four distinct tornadoes embedded within the system as it moved through Platte and Colfax counties. The sequence began southwest of Cornlea with an EF-1 tornado (104 mph peak winds) that unroofed a shed, snapped power poles, and flipped two center-pivot irrigation systems before lifting near Humphrey. A brief EF-0 tornado (65 mph peak winds) then tracked over three miles through cornfields southeast of Humphrey. Further east, a stronger EF-1 tornado (110 mph peak winds) touched down southwest of Leigh, snapping over a dozen trees at a cemetery and demolishing a large machine shed before clipping the town's southeast edge. Shortly after, another short-track EF-1 tornado (95 mph peak winds) set down on the west side of the Club 91 Golf Course in Colfax County. Moving northeast, it crossed Road V where concentrated tree damage occurred, continued across the pond on the north side of the baseball field producing additional tree damage, and finally lifted after crossing West Fork Maple Creek.||Surrounding the tornadic tracks, intense straight-line wind damage spanned the entirety of the storm corridor. Early in the event, estimated 74 mph winds downed large tree limbs near Lindsay, while severe gusts overturned a semi-truck south of Norfolk. As the complex moved through Colfax and Cuming counties, winds estimated between 70 and 74 mph overturned center pivots near Clarkson and downed large trees in Howells and Leigh, where fallen utility lines forced the closure of Church Street. Cuming County bore severe straight-line impacts, including a peak measured wind gust of 77 mph southeast of West Point; continuous swaths of snapped power poles, damaged farm outbuildings, stripped crops, and downed tree limbs were reported from Dodge northeast through West Point toward Uehling.
episodes.217433: This event continued the excessively active weather week from August 9th through the 15th. This event, and the event the followed just 24 hours later, brought excessive rainfall to Iowa and Illinois, especially south of Interstate 80, were four day rainfall totals of 4 to 10 inches were reported.|This was the 4th severe weather event in a period of near daily severe weather that extended through August 15th over eastern Iowa, Illinois, and northeast Missouri. This long duration of active weather was supported by a stationary front over the area, with heat, and exceptionally high levels of moisture.  Daily weak disturbances triggered storms.
episodes.217482: Afternoon and evening thunderstorms caused areas of flash flooding across the region.
episodes.217495: Afternoon and evening monsoon thunderstorms created more heavy rain and another round of flash flooding.
episodes.217709: On August 13th, strong heating under ridging created enough surface based instability to pulse up storms inland that moved southeasterly into inland southeast Georgia in the afternoon. Slightly drier air increased the chance of downbursts (DCAPE 1000 J/kg) especially along boundary collisions. On August 14th, ���heat wave��� ridging over the southeastern U.S. combined with a deeply moist and unstable airmass triggered pulse thunderstorms and sea breeze thunderstorms to develop in the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.217857: A low pressure trough along the west coast and high pressure positioned to the east over eastern Texas allowed deep monsoonal moisture to continue to surge northward out of Arizona with precipitable water increasing to over an inch. Dynamic support increased a bit more to allow for more widespread thunderstorm activity, with thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall rates that resulted in debris flows across portions of western Colorado.
episodes.217865: Since 2011, Suicide Basin, a side valley that is dammed by the Mendenhall Glacier, fills with water from snowmelt and rainfall then drains during the summer as a glacial outburst flood. This year, the glacier dammed lake in Suicide Basin, much like in 6 previous years (2018, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025), filled to the top of the Mendenhall Glacier (top of the ice dam) and began flowing down a side drainage channel on August 11th. While it has traditionally taken up to six days in past years for subglacial drainage to begin, the subglacial release this year started within just a few hours of the basin reaching capacity and overflowing the dam. Detecting the subglacial release was straightforward using cameras focused on the overflow channel, aided by favorable weather conditions with no rainfall.||The USGS laser sensor within the basin started to indicate a slow water level drop in the morning of August 11th and by the afternoon the drop in water increased with a rise starting on the Mendenhall Lake gauge. USGS Mendenhall Lake gauge, started to rise rapidly by the afternoon of August 12th. Through the evening and overnight hours, the river levels rose above the minor flood stage of 9.0ft. The Mendenhall Lake gauge continued to steadily rose through early Thursday morning of August 13th with the rate of rise increasing exponentially as the inflow to the lake from Suicide Basin was getting larger. Through the course of this glacier dam outburst flooding event, Mendenhall Lake and River rose more than 10 feet over a little more than two days and it crested at 14.71 ft on Thursday afternoon August 13th. This crest was the 4th highest on record. This flooding event caused major flooding impacts over a small area on the upstream side of Mendenhall Loop Road bridge near View Drive and the Mendenhall Lake. There was a larger area of moderate flooding impacts, mainly in places near flood protecting measures. These impacts were not as widespread as last year's event due to flood mitigation actions and a lower crest.
episodes.217955: Shortwave energy rounding the northern periphery of high pressure encountered an environment displaying large downdraft cape and an inland moving sea breeze locally, supporting thunderstorms capable of producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.217957: On August 12th, the region was under deep and unstable northwesterly flow and moist airmass. A passing upper shortwave triggered a convergent zone of numerous thunderstorms for locations from Waycross southeastward to the I-10 corridor. Stronger storms developed along this zone and along outflow boundary collisions. On August 13th, strong heating under ridging created enough surface based instability to pulse up storms inland that moved southeasterly into inland southeast Georgia in the afternoon. Slightly drier air increased the chance of downbursts (DCAPE 1000 J/kg) especially along boundary collisions.
episodes.218009: Northwest flow pattern coupled with a summer like environment helped spark scattered showers and thunderstorms. Of these, only isolated damaging winds and flash flooding occurred.
episodes.218073: Shortwave energy rounding the northern periphery of high pressure encountered an environment displaying large downdraft cape and an inland moving sea breeze locally, supporting thunderstorms capable of producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.218142: A subtropical high built across the central U.S. with weak troughing off the western U.S. coastline. This set the stage for robust moisture return into Utah, resulting in multiple instances of flash flooding across various locations in Utah. Across northern Utah, this system spawned a supercell which produced multiple instances of flash flooding across Tooele and Salt Lake counties, as well as numerous strong to significant severe wind gusts, large hail, and a tornado near the Skull Valley area in Tooele county.
episodes.218158: Scattered showers and thunderstorms fired off along the HWY60 corridor on the evening of the 13th. An isolated storm fire further south over Donley County and produced damaging winds. s. These downbursts from this storm were measured in the 60-70 mph range by local ground stations in Donley County, Texas. ||During the late afternoon of the 14th, high atmospheric moisture continued with a line of storms forming just north of the HWY60 corridor. A mesonet station located in Lipscomb County measured a wind gust of 65 mph from this line of storms. ||On the evening of the 15th, storms over parts of CO and NM moved southeast into the combined Panhandles. Additional scattered storms formed all across the OK Panhandle as well but it was the system that moved in from the northwest that produced a 61 mph at the Boise City, OK mesonet.
episodes.218163: The combination of cool west-northwest winds and a surface trough over the warm waters of Lake Erie led to some lake enhanced rain showers across the Pennsylvania waters of Lake Erie during the morning of August 13. Several waterspouts were reported with these showers offshore of North East, PA shortly before 9:00 AM.
episodes.218306: Shortwave moved through in the morning on Thursday, August 13th, into the afternoon, bringing morning showers across the north. Another round of shortwaves moved through in the afternoon into the evening. Storms developed in the north and in the Central Highlands and Bangor regions, through the evening. Ample instability resulted in frequent lightning, and gusty winds. Some storms in Penobscot county produced quarter-to-half inch sized hail. Storms weakened as the surface front passed after midnight.
episodes.218321: An active and stormy period resulted in another day of scattered thunderstorms. One cluster became severe late in the day with severe storm winds in Hawkins County.
episodes.218377: Isolated thunderstorms developed across upstate South Carolina during the late afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Greenville and Laurens Counties.
episodes.218405: Shortwave energy rounding the northern periphery of high pressure encountered an environment displaying large downdraft cape and an inland moving sea breeze locally, eventually supporting thunderstorms capable of producing damaging wind gusts across coastal waters.
episodes.218454: Some flooding occurred northwest of Poplar in Jefferson and Madison Counties near Heise.  Snake River Road washed out in Madison County with debris and East Heise Road closed east of Heise bridge to Kelly Canyon road due to water, mud and debris on the road.  Both floods were due to the Big Bock burn scar.
episodes.218489: Isolated thunderstorms developed over the Piedmont and foothills and western North Carolina during the afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.218507: Late afternoon pop up thunderstorms resulted in a severe wind gust in southern Ford County. A late evening MCS moved northeastward across western Kansas bringing a couple severe wind reports into western Kansas.
episodes.218508: On August 13th a pre-frontal trough and differential heating boundaries near the coast triggered thunderstorm development.  There was enough deep layer shear to allow a few storm to become organized with a very strong cell that traveled just south of Portland Maine and caused significant tree damage due gusts topping 70 mph.
episodes.218573: Thunderstorms across San Bernardino in southeastern California resulted in flash flooding and severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
episodes.218574: Monsoon moisture resulted in an isolated thunderstorm in Clark County in southern Nevada that produced severe winds.
episodes.218591: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred in association with a convective cloud line near the Lower Florida Keys.

Strong to locally severe thunderstorms trained over the Quartzsite area, generating heavy rainfall for an extended period and triggering widespread flash flooding. Radar estimates from Yuma, AZ Radar showed a widespread swath of 2 to 4 inches of rain falling within a three-hour time span. The flooding severely impacted local transportation, infrastructure, and businesses. Interstate 10 between Mile Markers 17 and 19 was closed for several hours as several inches of water flowed across the highway. Overflowing washes inundated numerous low-water crossings and video footage captured several inches of fast-moving water sweeping through local RV parks, with a photo showing an RV trailer swept away and found along Tyson Wash, the primary wash through Quartzsite, just south of interstate 10. Water and mud runoff caused significant damage to several establishments, including the Quartzsite Gem and Mineral Club, the Quartzsite Historical Society Museum, and Silly Al's Pizzeria. Although most of the floodwaters had receded by the following morning, photos revealed a light flow persisting in Tyson Wash along with residual mud and debris scattered across the area. Although not confirmed if the flooding was the main culprit, a broken main water line caused a total water service outage in Quartzsite. The damage cost was estimated at $100,000.  No injuries were reported.

Peak wind gusts were estimated upwards of 60 mph. Timing estimated from radar. No injuries reported.

The river continued to rise to a crest near 20.5 feet early the next morning, then receded below flood stage in the afternoon. While the river was out of its banks, flooding took place of low areas, campgrounds, and private camps along the river between Athens and Coolville. Flooding also occurred along Harmony Road. In Nelsonville, the baseball fields adjacent to Lake Hope Drive and Watkins Street also flooded.

A series of severe downbursts caused intermittent damage to trees and agricultural fields, snapped power poles, damaged at least one home, and blew the roof off of one barn. The maximum damage intensity appears to be in line with winds estimated at 90 mph, and extended from an area approximately 3 miles north northwest of Dodge through the far southern side of West Point. There were additional reports of damage east of West Point. While the peak damage intensity areas were intermittent, there were no clearly identifiable signs of focused rotation tracks within the broader downburst area. Numerous cornfields were impacted, and the corn damage was all pointing in the same southwest-to-northeast direction and sporadically spread across significant widths of the field. Tree branches also blew in that direction (southwest to northeast). The severe downburst damage was at times up to 4 miles wide.

The level of Mendenhall Lake was below normal for this time of year and was flowing just below 4 feet due to dry and cool conditions leading up to this event. It was detected that the sub-glacier release started in the morning of August 11th and by the afternoon hours water from the basin started to influence the Mendenhall Lake and the water levels in the lake began to rise. By the afternoon of Wednesday August 12th the rate of rise began to increase significantly, but at this time the water levels in Mendenhall Lake were below action stage of 8.0 feet. As the rate of rise increased through Wednesday evening the USGS Mendenhall Lake gauge went above the minor flood stage of 9 feet and then over moderate flood stage of 10ft at 125am AKDT on August 13th. By this time, areas near Skaters Cabin Rd and the Mendenhall Glacier Visitor Center were experiencing moderate flooding impacts with the USFS Mendenhall Lake Campground being evacuated. As water levels continued to rise, homes along View Drive were cut off with flood waters from 1 to 2 feet deep. The rate of rise was around a 2000 CFS increase per hour through the early morning hours. This rate of release was much slower than in the previous 2 years. The water levels reached 14ft, major flood stage, at 1130am AKDT on Thursday August 13th.  The river continued to rise but the rate started to slow around after noon and between 2 to 215pm AKDT the Mendenhall Lake gauge crested at 14.71 feet (preliminary crest from the USGS). This was the fourth highest crest in the period of record but lower than the 3 previous years first outburst flooding events. ||The Mendenhall Lake gauge was back below the moderate flood stage of 10ft at 725pm AKDT and below the minor flood stage of 9.0ft by 9pm AKDT on Thursday August 13th. The river system was above flood stage for nearly 24 hours. According to the City and Borough of Juneau (CBJ), this flooding event produced major impacts upstream of the Back Loop Road Bridge, along with minor impacts downstream along the Mendenhall River. These impacts below back loop bridge are similar to last year's, including some seepage through and damage to the flood protection barriers, but not as significant due to a much lower crest. Based on FEMA damage definitions, CBJ identified 10 homes as affected, including 2 with minor damage. The limited severity of impacts was due to the lower crest height, mentioned before, but also from improved personal flood protection along View Drive. Along the View Drive area, CBJ reported 2 homes sustained minor damage after 1���3 FT of water entered living spaces. Additional homes along Meander Way (5 -10) were also affected, caused by water seeping under or through HESCO barriers (flood protection measures) which minorly impacted those homes.
